activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister.
story:
The television above the kitchen doorway was on with the sound off, as it always was during dinner, and Brooklyn watched the anchor's mouth open and close while her father asked Maxim to pass the potatoes. Maxim had come over to finish their shared assignment for Mr. Ferreira's class, a position paper due by eight o'clock that night, and somehow the paper had turned into an argument that followed them to the table.

"You can't run for office and own the airwaves at the same time," Maxim said, sawing at his chicken. "That's not complicated. It's just obvious."

Kassidy, who had invited herself for the meatloaf, rolled her eyes so far Brooklyn thought she might see the wall behind her. "It's more complicated than obvious. Owners of newspapers endorse candidates. Nobody faints."

"That's different," Maxim said, and then, when Kassidy demanded how, he said, "It just is," which Brooklyn privately considered the weakest sentence in the English language.

The assignment asked them to take a position on whether a politician should ever be allowed to own a TV network. Mr. Ferreira had given them one week and a warning: whatever you argue, he had said, find one case that complicates it. Brooklyn had been putting off that part, and now it was almost six, and the paper needed two more pages. She ate quickly and watched the screen above her father's head. A commercial came on for the phone company he worked for, forty cheerful seconds of families video-calling each other.

Upstairs afterward, with the door open so her mother could hear they were behaving, Brooklyn opened her laptop and typed the words she'd been avoiding: politician owns TV network. The search results filled the screen. Italy. A man named Silvio Berlusconi, who kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister. She read the line twice, then read it aloud to the room.

"Three of them," Maxim said. "Three national channels. While he was prime minister."

"He won elections anyway," Kassidy said, reading over Brooklyn's shoulder. "Over and over. So the voters knew, and they picked him. Doesn't that mean it's their call?"

Maxim's shoulders were set in the obdurate way he got when a fact refused to bend around his opinion, and for a while he didn't say anything at all. Brooklyn started typing, then stopped. Her father worked for the phone company; the phone company bought advertising; the station running those ads was owned by a company with its own interests, and she had watched that station every night of her childhood without once wondering who owned it. She had thought of the news as a window, and it might be more like a lens, ground to somebody's prescription.

"It doesn't have to be a conspiracy," she said slowly. "You don't have to imagine anyone lying. You just have to notice what gets covered and what doesn't, and who benefits from the noticing." Maxim made a noise that suggested this was semantics, the same argument wearing a different sweater, but he didn't leave the room, which with Maxim counted as progress.

The clock said 7:15. Brooklyn took over the keyboard because Maxim typed like a man searching for each letter individually, and she wrote the paragraph that mattered: that a free press and a self-interested press could look identical from the couch, that the Italian case showed a leader holding both jobs at once, and that her own position had shifted from "ban it outright" to something less tidy. Regulate it, disclose it, and teach people to ask who holds the deed. Maxim objected that this was a retreat dressed up as nuance, and Kassidy said it was the first honest thing anyone had said all evening, and the two of them started in again while Brooklyn kept typing.

At 7:52 she uploaded the file. Maxim, reading over her shoulder, went quiet in a different way than before, and then said, "Fine. Disclosure beats prohibition. I was wrong to want it simple." He sounded almost cheerful about it, the way he always sounded once an argument had stopped being work.

Downstairs the television was still murmuring with the sound turned low now, and her father called up that the eleven o'clock broadcast was doing a segment on media consolidation, and did they want to watch it before bed. Brooklyn looked at the screen, at the anchor's calm face, and realized she didn't know which company was behind it. She got out her phone and started typing.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and ambition, and Grace stood at the counter with her mother's debit card in her pocket, reading a screen that promised her everything and obligated her to more. The salesclerk, a man with a lanyard and the patience of someone paid hourly, slid a tablet toward her and tapped a button marked Continue. "These are the terms and conditions," he said. "You sign here, we ship the phone tomorrow, and your plan starts at thirty dollars a month." Grace looked at the signature line, thin and waiting, the way a held breath is waiting.

She was here because her old phone had died on Tuesday, mid-message, while she was tutoring Izabella in chemistry over video call for the fourth time that month. That was the arrangement, allegedly. Izabella had texted her the first week: "ok but you have to let me pay you, like 15 an hour, i insist." Grace had replied that she didn't care, and Izabella had replied with three fire emojis, which in their shared language meant binding. Then yesterday, a different message: "hey so my mom says tutoring from a friend doesn't really count, you know? like it's not a real thing. sorry. you're still coming sunday though right." Grace had read it four times, once in each tone available to her: hurt, amused, legalistic, tired.

At the counter, the clerk was saying something about liability. "If the phone is lost in shipping, that's on us for the first thirty days. After that, it's on you, unless you add the protection plan, which is nine ninety-nine a month." He said it the way a person recites a bedtime prayer, and Grace noticed that everything here had this quality: each sentence was a little machine with two sides, something given, something taken. The store offered a phone. She would accept by signing. She would pay thirty dollars a month, and the company would give her service. Each side gave something of value in exchange. That was the whole cathedral of it, apparently, and people walked through it daily without looking up.

She thought about it while the clerk ran the card. Backwards, almost, the way she did when a problem refused to sit still, and she was aware of doing it, which her psychology teacher had called metacognition and which Grace privately called noticing yourself being difficult. In common-law countries like this one, a contract generally needed three things: an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange. Izabella had offered fifteen an hour. Had Grace accepted? She'd said she didn't care, which was acceptance the way a shrug is a handshake. But consideration: Izabella had never actually paid anything, and money was the entire point of a promise to pay. A promise against nothing. The clerk's tablet would never have processed it. Somewhere in the machinery of the law, Izabella's fire emojis had failed to load.

"Can I see that protection plan thing again?" Grace asked. The clerk blinked, mildly betrayed. She had already declined it twice, having decided that nine ninety-nine a month to insure a phone she could not afford to lose anyway was a philosophy of despair. But her mother's voice had come back to her on the drive over, some antiquated wisdom about how the day you skip the insurance is the day the phone goes in the lake, and Grace had learned, recently, that being eighteen meant conducting these small negotiations between the person she'd been and the person signing things. She added the plan. Her monthly total transfigured from manageable to aspirational. She signed, four times, which seemed excessive for one phone.

On Sunday she tutored Izabella anyway, at the kitchen table, because Izabella's mother made lemonade and because the exam was Wednesday and because that was, Grace had decided, the actual contract. Not the one with the fire emojis. The unwritten one, where Izabella's mother had driven Grace home every session since September, and where nobody kept score because keeping score would ruin it. Izabella opened her chem textbook and said, "Are you still mad about the money thing?" and Grace said, "It was never a contract, there was no consideration," and Izabella said, "You sound like a phone store," and they both laughed, and it was not entirely a joke.

What Grace couldn't settle, in the days after, was which arrangement was the safer one. The tablet's contract would survive a falling-out, would survive Izabella moving to a different city, would compel thirty dollars a month out of her for two years whether she loved the phone or not. The kitchen-table one bound nobody. Izabella could stop showing up tomorrow, and Grace would have no signature to wave at her, only a season of lemonade and stoichiometry already spent. She held both ideas at once the way you hold two phones, one in each hand, and did not drop either.

Wednesday night, after the exam, her new phone buzzed. It was Izabella: "got a 92. my mom put twenty in an envelope for you, she says no arguments." Grace typed "you can't do that, there was no consideration" and then deleted it, and typed "tell her thank you," and then deleted that too, and sat looking at the signature-blue glow of the screen. She set the phone face down on her desk and went to find the envelope.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The screen door of Ms. Grant's house banged twice before Zoe got it to close, and the noise of the living room swallowed the second bang anyway. Twenty people were packed onto a sagging sectional and a ring of folding chairs, all of them watching the neighbor's enormous television, because Ms. Grant had the biggest screen on the street and the only air conditioning that worked. The game was in its final minutes, tied, and Zoe's father had claimed the good armchair an hour ago and refused to move since.

She found Anson by the snack table, holding a bowl of chips like a shield. "You're late," he said. "You missed your dad lionizing the referee. He thinks the man should have a statue in the town square. Or be burned in effigy. He wasn't clear."

"I was helping Ms. Grant carry the cooler." Zoe took a handful of chips and wedged herself onto the arm of the couch beside Noa, who had been saving the spot with a folded sweater. On the screen, a striker tumbled in the box, the crowd roared, the referee pointed to the spot, and the whole room surged to its feet except Zoe, who had seen the replay. The defender had gotten the ball first, cleanly, and she said so, quietly, and Noa shushed her.

Then the referee touched his ear and drew a rectangle in the air, and everything stopped. The players stood around the penalty area with their hands on their hips. The commentators filled the silence with the word VAR, over and over, and Zoe felt the room lean toward the television as one body.

"It's the video assistant referee," Noa said to Ms. Grant, who had come in from the kitchen with a tray of cups and was frowning at the frozen players. "They're checking the monitor."

"I know what it is," Zoe said. "This is the first World Cup they've used it. In Russia, this summer. That's why nobody knew what to expect." She had read everything she could find before the tournament, partly to argue with her father, who claimed the checks would ruin the game, and partly because she liked knowing the edges of a rule. "They can review goals, penalties, straight red cards, and cases of mistaken identity."

"Mistaken identity," Anson repeated, delighted. "They gave a red card to the wrong twin."

"That's not why the rule exists."

"It could be, though."

The wait stretched. Someone's uncle groaned that this was why he'd stopped watching, that a game you could finish in ninety minutes now took all night, and Zoe's father turned around in the armchair and said, without heat, "Tell her, Zoe. Tell him what else they can review." She could hear the pride in it and it embarrassed her, the way it always did, and she recited the list again, flat, like reading a bus schedule, and the uncle waved her off.

What she didn't say, because there was no room for it in a loud room, was that she had spent the whole tournament arguing both sides in her head. Her father wanted the game left alone, human and flawed, errors part of its charm, the way a garden is part of a house. Anson wanted every call right, every dive punished, every injustice corrected while the world watched. Zoe had started out on her father's side, mostly to be contrary, and then a goal she'd celebrated for a full minute had been chalked off in the group stage, and she'd felt the strange reprieve of it, the suspended justice, and thought maybe Anson was right that certainty beat joy. Now she sat on the arm of the couch with no side at all, only the suspicion that both of them wanted something the other couldn't see, and that she wanted both things too.

The verdict came. The referee crossed his arms, cancelled the penalty, and the room erupted, half in fury and half in vindication, and Zoe's father rose from his chair to accept congratulations as though he had personally reviewed the footage. "See? The system works," Anson shouted over the din, pointing at the screen, and Zoe was about to answer that one reversed call proved nothing either way when the corner was taken, poorly cleared, and a midfielder she'd never heard of struck the ball through a crowd of legs and into the net at the far post.

The room went silent for one full second, waiting for the rectangle in the air. It didn't come. The referee pointed to the center circle and the goal stood, and Ms. Grant, whose team it was, set down her tray and put both hands over her mouth. Zoe's father sat back down very slowly. Anson slid the chip bowl onto the table, and Zoe watched the replays stack up on the giant screen, one angle after another, and realized she was already looking for the offside line herself, drawing it in her mind, before the memory of what she'd believed an hour ago had even finished fading.

"You okay?" Noa asked.

"Watching," Zoe said, eyes still on the screen.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
Chase sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with Jane Eyre open to a page he had read three times, a legal pad beside it, a whiteboard borrowed from the den propped against the salt shaker and the sugar bowl. The assignment was due Monday, and Monday was close enough now that he could feel it in his shoulders. Ms. Anderson had asked for a Marxist reading of one passage, any passage, and had said only, "Ask who owns what, and who works." He had underlined that twice on the sheet.

The passage he'd chosen was the one where Jane first arrives at Thornfield, the housekeeper showing her through the halls, the servants moving out of her way. It had seemed rich to him at first, and then it had gone slippery every time he tried to say something about it. He had written "class stuff happens" on the legal pad and crossed it out, which was the sum of his progress so far.

The house smelled of his grandfather's coffee and the lemon polish his grandmother used on the banister, though she had been gone two years and he only polished it now when he visited, out of habit or grief. Outside, the maple had begun dropping its keys on the porch. Chase wrote "Thornfield" at the top of the whiteboard and underlined it, then drew two lines beneath, dividing the space into halves he did not yet know how to fill.

He started naming characters. Rochester went on the first line. Then he paused, marker uncapped, because the second line needed a label and he did not have one. He texted Miah, who had taken the same class last semester and owed him for a ride to the lake in June.

Miah called instead of texting back. "You're sorting people into owners and workers," she said when he explained. "It's the Marxist thing. The bourgeoisie owns the means of production, like factories and land. The proletariat owns only its labour, and has to sell it for wages."

"So Rochester's bourgeoisie," Chase said, drawing the word out phonetically under the first line. "He owns the house, the land, the mill money. And the servants go under proletariat because all they've got to sell is their work."

"And Jane," Miah said. "Don't forget Jane. That's your whole paper, honestly."

He wrote Jane's name on the second line and then sat looking at it, because she did not fit cleanly. She had been sent to Thornfield to sell her labour, that was true, her wages were even named in the passage, thirty pounds a year. But the housekeeper treated her as neither family nor servant, and Jane herself kept insisting on her mind, her feelings, things that belonged to no one but her. He crossed Jane's name out and wrote it again, smaller, directly on the line between the two halves.

"Is that allowed?" Miah asked when he described it. She was laughing a little, not unkindly. "Putting her on the border?"

"I don't know. It's the honest place for her."

They talked a while longer, and after he hung up he worked. He filled the second line with the cook, the maid, the unnamed man who drove the carriage, and next to Rochester he wrote "owns the means of production" in his smallest hand, so the fact of it stayed on the board. Then he found he could not leave the border alone. Jane's position there was not confusion, he decided, or not only confusion. The novel kept asking whether a person could be more than what she had to sell, and the Marxist lens kept answering, in its patient grinding way, that under this arrangement nobody was allowed to be. He thought of the word ontology, which Ms. Anderson had used once in class, what a thing is in its being, and wrote in the margin: under wages, what you are is what you can sell. He liked that. He also suspected it was not quite fair to Jane, who kept being more than her situation in ways the lens could register only as noise.

Alessio arrived at four to return a lacrosse stick he had borrowed in June, found Chase surrounded by index cards, and read the whiteboard over his shoulder with his coat still on. "You've expropriated my boy Rochester," he said. "Stripped him of everything but his property."

"That's the point, kind of," Chase said. "You sort them and then you see what the sorting can't hold."

Alessio tapped the border where Jane's name sat. "This line though. You're going to hand in a diagram with a person sitting on a fence?"

"It's inchoate," Chase said. "I know that. It's the best part of it and the worst part." He capped the marker and stood at the window while Alessio warmed his hands at the stove. The maple keys lay across the porch boards, dozens of them, spinning down all afternoon, and Chase watched a few more let go of the branch.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
Laurence held her cup of punch and rehearsed her handshake on a balloon, which popped, and Mrs. Okafor's spaniel raced under the folding table with the ribbon. Sixteen guests turned to look. "Practicing for an interview," she announced, as though that explained the dog, the balloon, and the fact that she was standing in Matilda's kitchen wearing her grandmother's idea of interview clothes, which was a blazer two sizes stern.

The job was at Hollis Books, three afternoons a week after school, and the interview was Monday at four. The trouble was not the resume, which Matilda's older sister had formatted with alarming competence. The trouble was her grandmother, who had arrived on a sabbatical from her university post in Seoul and had opinions, and her mother, who had opinions about the opinions. On Friday they had staged a coaching session over dumplings that ended with Laurence staring at the ceiling to avoid offending either of them.

"You must look at the interviewer," her mother had said, tapping the table with her chopsticks for emphasis. "Steady eye contact. It shows confidence here. They expect it."

Her grandmother had set down her tea. "When I interviewed for the department, I looked at the teapot. The senior professor, you do not stare at him like that. Prolonged direct gaze at a senior person, it can seem impolite. You show respect differently."

"Mom, this is a bookstore in Brampton."

"Bookstores have seniors too," her grandmother had said serenely, and refused to elaborate, and Laurence had spent the weekend stuck between the two like a spectator at a tennis match played entirely in glances.

At the party, Abigale was stacking cups into a tower and narrating the structural failures like a sports announcer. Laurence externalized her dilemma the only way she knew how, which was to dramatize it: she fixed Abigale with an unblinking stare, said "I am a confident candidate," then dropped her eyes to the floor tiles and murmured the same sentence at them. "Pick one," she begged. "Which am I?"

Abigale laughed so hard the tower collapsed. "You look like a heron with the second one. Very respectful heron."

"Help me, though. Seriously. Monday."

Ms. Quinn, who lived next door to Matilda and had drifted in with a plate of lemon squares, folded herself into a lawn chair by the snack table. She was between contracts, Matilda had said, something in consulting, and she watched Laurence's heron performance with her chin in her hand. "Do it again," she said, and Laurence did, confident gaze first, floor gaze second. Ms. Quinn made a noncommittal sound through the lemon square. Then she asked where Laurence's family was from, and Laurence said her mother grew up here and her grandmother had spent thirty years in Seoul, and something in Ms. Quinn's face went quiet and interested at once.

"You know," Ms. Quinn said, "I worked with a team in Seoul for a year, and then a team in Toronto the year after. Both were hiring. The Toronto managers wrote 'poor eye contact, weak presence' about candidates who'd have interviewed beautifully in the Seoul office. And the Seoul seniors thought the visiting Canadians stared like owls." She dusted sugar off her fingers. "It's not about courage. It's about which room you're in."

"So which room is Hollis Books?" Laurence asked.

"That," said Ms. Quinn, "is the whole question, and it's yours."

Laurence thought about it while Matilda led an effort to rescue the spaniel, and by the time the cake came out she had worked out something she could hold onto without pretending the uncertainty away. Hollis Books was in Brampton. The interviewer would be, in all likelihood, someone local, someone expecting the North American style, so on Monday she would look up, hold the gaze, speak clearly. But it was not a universal law, only a local one, a guess about the room; if the interviewer ever turned out to be someone who found steady staring forward and impolite, she would know why, and she would not think the woman was weak, and she would not think she herself had failed. Her mother's advice and her grandmother's advice were both true somewhere. The skill was telling the somewheres apart.

On Monday at four she walked into Hollis Books wearing the stern blazer, and the manager, a young woman with a lanyard and a stack of returns, said, "Laurence? Ready?" Laurence looked her in the eye and said, "Yes, I'm ready," and her gaze did not waver, except once, briefly and on purpose, when the woman's boss leaned around the corner to see who had come in.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
Nicolas had the whiteboard on his lap in the rink's meeting room, drawing arrows that all ended in the same place, which was the problem. Every arrow he drew got swallowed by the little X's of the defending forwards. Mr. Ramos had given him the novice team on Tuesday and said almost nothing since, only that Nicolas should find one weakness and fix it, one, as if that instruction circumscribed the whole job.

He watched from the bench during the scrimmage on Thursday. Peyton-like kids, nine and ten years old, kept slapping the puck cross-ice, and every time a defender's stick lay flat on the ice the puck died there like a bug on a windshield. Three breakout attempts, three blocked passes, and then a fourth where the winger just gave the puck away out of pure discouragement.

"That's it," he said to Felicia, who was sorting pucks into a bucket with more attention than pucks required. "Nobody's getting a pass through."

"So tell them to pass harder."

"Speed doesn't fix it. The stick is on the ice. The puck is on the ice. It's like a fence." He turned his pen over in his hands. He was eighteen and had played this game for twelve years and had taken a thousand saucer passes without once asking what he was doing.

He remembered being ten himself, in this same rink, standing at the far blue line while his own coach skated out with a single puck and no speech. His coach had flipped the puck once, casually, so it lifted a few inches, sailed flat over the stick of the defenceman he'd planted there, and dropped onto Nicolas's blade without a bounce. He had forgotten it entirely until now, standing on the other side of the glass.

At Friday's practice he set up the drill before the kids came on. One line of passers, one line of receivers, and between them a rigid plastic stick bolted to a low stand, lying flat across the lane like a gate. He didn't explain anything. He put a puck on the first kid's stick and said, "Get it to your teammate."

The first pass thudded into the barrier. The second, the fourth, the sixth. Then Leila's little brother, a small stubborn kid named only as Declan to the team but listed on the roster as D. Okafor, opened his blade, rolled his wrists, and the puck rose just off the ice, flew flat over the gate, and landed cleanly on the receiver's blade. Half the parents in the stands made the sound parents make.

"That's a saucer pass," Nicolas said, loud enough for the whole line. "Again."

The boy couldn't repeat it, not exactly. Nicolas skated out and tried it himself and found he couldn't teach it with words either; when he said "open the face" the kids angled their blades skyward and the puck climbed like a pop fly and landed with a clattering, useless bounce. He stood there with his helmet off, breathing cold rink air, thinking about modularity, a word from his engineering elective. He had planned the drill as a module, a sealed little unit: weakness, solution, rep. But the pass wasn't a module. It was a judgment the wrists made in a fraction of a second about height and distance, and the drill could only build the conditions for it, not the thing itself.

He rebuilt the drill twice more that hour. First he lowered the gate so that even a bad flip cleared it, and the kids succeeded constantly, but he suspected that success was a pernicious comfort, because they weren't learning to keep the pass flat, only to lob. Then he raised it slightly and made the receivers call the pass early, and something better happened: the passes got flatter. He couldn't have said why. Maybe the receiver's voice gave the passer a target tighter than the whole lane.

Afterward Mr. Ramos came down from the stands with his coat on. "Next week, same thing?"

"I think so. Maybe." Nicolas looked at the gate bolted to the stand, at the arc of melted snow the Zamboni hadn't reached. "I fixed the drill twice tonight. I don't know which one was right. I don't even know if right is the word."

Mr. Ramos looked at the ice for a while. "The kids who got better, did they know they were doing it right?"

"No. They just did it."

"Then run it again and find out." He zipped his coat and went toward the parking lot, and Nicolas stood a moment longer, watching the meltwater run down the boards toward the drain.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules and each enters the cycle separately.
story:
The lab smelled of graphite and the faint vinegar tang someone had spilled near the sink, and Alexandra counted on her fingers for the third time. Glycolysis: two ATP. The citric acid cycle: one ATP per turn. She wrote 3 on the worksheet, then crossed it out, because the answer key taped inside Ms. Ong's folder apparently said something in the twenties, and Alexandra could not find the missing twenty.

"You look like you're doing taxes," Shannon said, sliding onto the stool beside her. Shannon had finished her own worksheet in eleven minutes, which was either brilliance or a talent for writing plausible nonsense quickly, and Alexandra had never decided which.

"Count the ATP," Alexandra said. "From glucose to the end. I keep getting three, and that can't be right, because a cell would starve to death on three."

Ms. Ong moved between the benches in her diurnal circuit, morning through afternoon, checking notebooks the way a doctor checks pulses. She stopped at their table, looked at Alexandra's crossed-out numbers, and said nothing, which was her way of saying more. She tapped the diagram of the mitochondrion once, on the inner folded stratum of its membrane, and moved on.

"She does that," Mattias said from the next bench. He was leaning back with his pencil behind his ear, watching Alexandra the way he watched a chessboard when it was her move. "Taps something and leaves. It's like being blessed by a very small pope."

Alexandra looked at the diagram. She understood glycolysis, mostly: one glucose split into two smaller molecules, a small profit of ATP, everything else carried forward. What happened next had a name she'd copied off the board without feeling it, acetyl-CoA, and then the citric acid cycle, which she had drawn as a neat little circle with an arrow, one turn, one ATP.

She drew the arrow again and stopped. One glucose became two of those acetyl-CoA molecules, and each one entered the cycle separately. The circle turned once for the first, and then again for the second. The cycle turned twice for each glucose, and that was before whatever happened along that folded membrane Ms. Ong had tapped, which Shannon's notes claimed was where most of the energy actually got squeezed out.

"It turns twice," Alexandra said out loud. "Mattias. The cycle. Each glucose makes two acetyl-CoA, so each one goes in on its own. It turns twice."

Mattias pulled the pencil from behind his ear and redid his own tally, muttering. "I wrote one," he said. "I wrote one like an idiot." He crossed it out without ceremony, and Shannon leaned over to compare her sheet, found her own quiet mistake two lines down, and laughed at herself, not loudly, the way people do when the mistake is small and the relief is large.

Alexandra rewrote her count from the top, and the number climbed past three, past ten, into territory that made the whole machine seem suddenly worth running. Somewhere in the doubling she caught herself valuing the elegance of it more than the usefulness, the way their textbook seemed to valorize cleverness over the plain fact that cells needed dinner, and she hadn't yet decided whether that was a flaw in her or in the book. She wrote her final answer, checked it twice, and then slid the worksheet across to Shannon, whose face had gone uncertain near the bottom of the page.

"Count yours from glycolysis onward," Alexandra said. "Everything after it happens twice."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
The food bank shared the library's basement, and by nine on Saturday morning the folding tables were already up between the microfilm cabinets and the old atlas shelf. Olivier had signed up because his school required forty hours of something, and the library was the only place he could walk to. Mr. Takahashi, the head librarian, met him at the stairs with a clipboard and a hairnet, which Olivier took as a sign of how the day would go.

"You'll be on hampers," Mr. Takahashi said. "Breanna will show you the system."

Breanna was a girl from his grade he knew mostly as a name on attendance. She handed him a list printed on yellow paper. Each family had a number, not a name, and beside the number a count of adults, a count of children, and any notes. She showed him how to read the pantry shelves like sentences: pasta here, formula at the far end, snacks on the low shelf where the little kids who came with their parents could reach them.

The first hour was straightforward, almost pleasant, the work of matching boxes to lists. But by the fourth hamper Olivier had started keeping a private tally in his head, and by the tenth he had stopped tallying because the pattern was obvious. Baby cereal. Toddler pouches. Juice boxes. Granola bars sized for lunchboxes. Of the eleven hampers he'd packed, eight had a children's line at all, and nearly every one of those included something small and soft and specifically for a kid.

"Is it always like this?" he asked.

Breanna looked up from her clipboard. "Like what?"

"So many kids." He gestured at the low shelf, half-emptied now. "Baby food, snacks. I thought it would mostly be, I don't know, single guys. Old guys."

Jacob, working the intake table by the door, snorted without looking over. "That's what everyone thinks."

At the break, Olivier sat on the steps outside the basement door with his phone and texted his brother, who was at university and liked being asked things. Is it true that a lot of food bank users are kids? he typed. He ate half a granola bar from the volunteer box while he waited, and it tasted like the ones he used to find in his own lunch, which unsettled him in a way he decided not to examine yet.

His brother's reply came in pieces. Yes. Look up HungerCount. It's from Food Banks Canada. Their March 2025 report. Children were about one-third of food bank visits in Canada that month. A third. Let that sit. Olivier read the message twice, then a third time, and noticed he was ruminate-ing on it, turning the number over the way he turned over a line of poetry in English class, testing whether it meant what it appeared to mean. One in three. He thought of his homeroom of thirty. Ten of them.

Back inside, he checked the fact against his own tally, which was not science, he knew, just eleven boxes on one morning in one basement. Still, the two things rhymed. He found himself standing still between the shelves, holding a can of formula, and Mr. Takahashi passed by with a cart and said, "You're doing fine," as if Olivier had been worrying out loud.

A woman came in at eleven with a boy of about four who went straight to the low shelf and stood in front of the juice boxes with the patience of someone who knew the rules. Jacob greeted the mother by number. Breanna assembled their hamper. Olivier had no job that required him, so he crouched and offered the boy a choice between apple and fruit punch, and the boy chose with enormous gravity, and that was the whole exchange, and Olivier found he had to look at the shelving unit for a moment afterward.

Later, sweeping, he tried to hold two ideas at each other without letting either one flatten the other. The first was that a society where a third of food bank visits were children was a travesty, full stop, no argument. The second was that a food bank in a library basement, run by a librarian and two teenagers and a yellow-paper system that worked, was genuinely good, and he did not want his nascent indignation to swallow that up, because the good was real too. He couldn't get the two ideas into one sentence that satisfied him. Maybe they didn't fit in one sentence. Maybe they both just stood there, like the boy in front of the juice boxes.

At noon Mr. Takahashi signed his sheet and asked if he'd be back. Olivier said probably, meaning yes, and meaning also that he intended to find out how many Saturdays there were until June.

Outside, Breanna caught up with him on the sidewalk. "You looked like you were having a revelation down there," she said.

"Not a revelation. More like arithmetic." He zipped his jacket. "A third of the visits are kids. One in three."

Breanna nodded, unsurprised, and pointed down the block toward the bus stop. "Coming?"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The community center gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn, and Rachel had learned, over six weeks of Tuesdays and Thursdays, that the lights hummed at a pitch only noticeable when a rally stopped. Tonight the rally had stopped for good. Francis had spiked a warm-up ball into the back of Chayce's head, not on purpose but not entirely not on purpose, and now the whole team stood in a loose ring near the net while those two argued about whose fault the lost weekend tournament had been.

"You bailed on the play," Chayce said. "You always bail when it matters."

"That's not what happened and you know it," Francis said, and Rachel watched his knuckles whiten around the ball he refused to set down, the way a person holds something just to have something to hold.

The coach sent everyone to the bleachers to cool off, which was her solution to everything, and the team sat in a sullen row drinking from dented water bottles. Rachel pulled out her phone. Later she would not be able to say why she typed the words into the search bar, except that she had spent the drive here wondering whether other teams broke apart in the middle too, or whether hers was uniquely rotten. The gym's signal was bad, one bar that flickered like the lights, and the page loaded slowly, paragraph by paragraph.

Chayce leaned over, nosy by nature. "What are you reading?"

"Something weird," Rachel said, and turned the screen toward him. "This psychologist. Bruce Tuckman, in 1965. He said groups develop through four stages. Forming, storming, norming, performing." She said it flat, testing the words in her mouth, and watched his face do something complicated, relief arriving before he could decide whether to trust it.

"Storming," Francis repeated from three seats down, and he laughed once, short and surprised. "That's us. That's literally us, right now."

Rachel scrolled further, but the article said only what it said, no reasons, no map for getting out, and she found she preferred it that way, a fact without a cure. She thought of trying to exculpate Francis, to lay out for Chayce the sequence at the tournament where the missed rotation had actually started with Rachel's own short pass, but she stopped. Her evidence would not make the argument smaller. It would only spread it wider, and she wanted, sharply, to play volleyball in November.

"Okay," she said, standing. "So it has a name. That doesn't fix anything."

"It kind of does," Chayce said.

"It doesn't. It just means we're normal instead of broken." She looked at them both, at Francis still cradling the ball, at Chayce's jaw set in a line she privately called his intransigent line, the one he wore during budget meetings too, when he insisted on counting the fundraiser money twice because, as he put it, whoever held the cash was basically a fiduciary for the whole team and had to act like one. He had been right about that, and insufferable about it, and she noticed now that those two things seemed to travel together in him.

She walked to the middle of the court and started picking up the cones, because someone had to, and because her body wanted movement more than her mind wanted more talk. The lights hummed. After a moment Francis came down and took the other end of the net pole, loosening it the way the coach had taught them, and Chayce stood at the sideline with the ball, spinning it on one finger.

"If we're in the storming part," Chayce called out, "how do we know when it's over?"

"I don't know," Rachel said. "The article didn't say."

"That's a terrible article."

"It's an honest one."

The coach blew her whistle from the office doorway, two short blasts, the signal for ten more minutes of serve receive before the center closed. Rachel took her position behind the service line and bounced the ball once, twice, feeling the wax under her sneakers grip and release. Francis rotated into the back row beside her, close enough that she could hear him breathing. He set the seam between them with a small tilt of his head, the old signal, and she tilted hers back.

From across the court, Chayce cupped his hands. "Rachel. Serve it deep two."

She tossed the ball up.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
Alice had memorized the parking lot before she ever sat in the driver's seat, because for years it had been the place where the Saturday market set up its tents, and now, on a grey Tuesday evening, it was only herself, the car, and her grandfather's voice in her head. He had called that morning from two provinces away, expatiating on the art of driving as though forty years of it entitled him to a lecture: watch your mirrors, grip the wheel at ten and two, and if anything ever runs in front of you, pump the brakes. Pump them, he said, don't just stand on the pedal like a fool. She had said yes, Grandpa, three times, and then sat with the phone warm against her ear a moment longer, because he had taught her to ride a bike and she wanted him to be right about this too.

Maryam was in the back seat with her phone held sideways, which was not what Alice had asked for. Maryam wanted footage for the video montage she was making about their whole year, the last months of everything, and she had a way of framing every event as material before it had even happened. "You're not going to crash," she said now, leaning between the seats. "If you crash, I'll delete it. Scout's honour."

Ms. Das sat in the passenger seat with a clipboard she never wrote on. She had Alice start the engine, check the mirrors she'd already adjusted twice, and ease the car forward along the painted lines, and for ten minutes the lot was smooth grey asphalt and the small sounds of Alice correcting herself. Her turns were inchoate at first, wide then suddenly tight, the wheel feeling less like an instrument than like something she was negotiating with. Ms. Das said less than Alice expected. Left here. Straighten. Again.

Then, near the far end where the market's vegetable stalls used to run, a shopping cart stood loose in the lane, blown in from somewhere, bright red and absurd. Alice saw it late. Her foot went to the brake and her grandfather's voice arrived with it, and she began to lift and press, lift and press, pumping the way he'd told her, and the car kept travelling toward the cart with a strange independence, as if the braking belonged to someone else's decision.

"Hold it," Ms. Das said, calm, not loud. "Firm and hold. You've got anti-lock brakes; press firmly and hold it, and you can still steer."

Alice pressed down and kept pressing, and turned the wheel, and the car slowed and came around the cart with room to spare, stopping a little crooked but stopped. Her hands were shaking on the wheel. She hadn't hit anything, and the pedal had buzzed back at her under her foot, which she had not been warned about and which she decided not to mention.

"Grandpa said to pump," she said finally, because it seemed disloyal to let the silence decide the matter.

"He drove different cars," Ms. Das said. That was all, and Alice found she appreciated that it was all, that no one expatiated at her about it. In the back seat Maryam lowered her phone. "Okay, that was actually incredible," she said. "Can we do it again? Like, is there another cart?" She was already scanning the lot for props, because the montage wanted a climax and Maryam had been collecting climaxes all spring, every last this, every final that, hoarding endings the way other people hoarded beginnings. Alice understood it and resented it a little and depended on it a little, since someone had to remember things or they slipped.

The detraction she felt was small but real: her grandfather had taught her to ride a bike, had run behind her on the river path with one hand on the seat, and now there was a thing he had told her that was wrong, out of date, a rule from cars she'd never seen. It didn't cancel the path by the river. It sat beside it. She could not make the two line up, and she suspected she wasn't supposed to, that most of what people gave you came in versions like this, true once and partly true still. Even her detractors, she thought, and stopped herself, because that was the wrong word for a grandfather, and she laughed at herself for it, quietly, into her hand on the wheel.

"Once more around the lot," Ms. Das said, "then we switch seats and you watch me park, because watching is half the lesson." Alice put the car in drive. As they came back up the far lane she steered wide around the cart, giving it more room than it needed, and Maryam raised the phone again, and through the windshield the cart sat there red and still in the empty lot, waiting for nobody, going nowhere unless the wind decided otherwise.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
Nevaeh's poster board was propped on table fourteen, and the diagram of her parallel plates had the arrows pointing the wrong way, and judging began in forty minutes. She knew it was wrong because Tala had stopped in front of the board, squinted, and asked the one question Nevaeh could not answer.

"Which way would a proton move in there?" Tala tapped the gap between the plates.

"Left," Nevaeh said, because that was where her arrows pointed.

Tala folded her arms. "Your positive plate is on the left."

The gym smelled of floor wax and hot glue. Down the row a boy was stapling ferns to a corkboard, and near the doors Ms. Nguyen was walking the aisles with her clipboard, stopping at each table for a word with whoever stood behind it. Nevaeh had until she reached table fourteen to fix the arrows or to understand them, and she was not sure those were the same task.

Thierry was already crouched under the table, rigging the auxiliary battery pack she'd borrowed from the physics room, a second power source that could run the demo if the gym's outlet failed the way it failed last year. He emerged holding two wires. "Recidivism," he announced.

"What?"

"Last year the power died at regionals. The year before, the power died at regionals. If it happens again, that's recidivism. Repeat offending." He taped the battery to the table leg. "I refuse to let your project become a repeat offender."

"Thierry." She pointed at the diagram. "Which way do the arrows go?"

He stood, wiped his hands on his jeans, and looked. Then he looked longer than she wanted him to.

"Undo them," he said.

"No. Tell me."

"That's me telling you. I'm not going to pontificate at you about it, I don't have the whole thing straight myself, but I know they're backwards. Undo them and figure it out before Nguyen gets here."

She pulled the arrows off. They were just little paper triangles, the kind of thing that took ten minutes to draw and cut and pin, and now the space between her plates was empty, which felt like honesty and like ruin at the same time. The demo itself was still sound: two foil-covered boards, a charged ball of foil on a thread between them, a switch. The diagram was supposed to explain what the demo showed.

Tala was still there, arms still folded. "Walk me through it," she said. "The way you'd tell a judge."

"Two plates. One positive, one negative. The field is in the middle." That much Nevaeh knew cold; she had copied it from three sources and could recite it in her sleep. Reciting was not the problem.

"Okay. So the positive plate is on the left in your setup."

"Yes."

"So say the proton thing again."

"Positive charge moves left."

"Why?"

The question sat there. Behind them the fern boy dropped his stapler, and Ms. Nguyen's voice carried from table nine, patient and unhurried, which meant she was spending real time there, which meant Nevaeh had less than she'd thought. She looked at her own empty diagram, at the positive plate on the left and the negative plate on the right, and tried to picture a single proton dropped into the gap. A proton was positive. The positive plate was positive. She thought about magnets, about how you cannot push two north poles together, how your hands feel the refusal of it.

"It wouldn't move left," she said slowly. "The positive plate would push it away. Toward the negative one."

"So the field," Tala said.

"The field is the push. The direction a positive charge would be pushed." She heard herself say it and felt the click of it locking in, the arrows not as decoration but as an answer to Tala's question, drawn for a proton nobody would ever see. "So it points from the positive plate to the negative plate. That's the whole reason the arrows go that way. It's not a rule somebody made up to fail me. It's just where a proton would go."

"You should tell the judges exactly that," Tala said. "The question part especially. Judges like the question part."

Nevaeh drew fast, pen on paper, arrows marching from positive to negative, rightward, all of them, and she thought of the field as a slope a proton would slide down, though she kept that to herself because she wasn't yet sure the slope picture was fair and she didn't want to borrow certainty she hadn't earned. Some of it she still couldn't defend. Why the field was uniform in the middle, why the thread on her foil ball hung at an angle instead of swinging all the way over, she would say "I'm still working on that" if a judge asked, and she had decided that saying it was better than pretending.

"Seven minutes," Thierry said from under the table. He flipped the switch on the auxiliary pack, and the foil ball leaned sideways toward the negative plate, steady, obedient to something invisible that now, for the first time, she could name the direction of. She pinned the new diagram to the board, arrows and all.

Ms. Nguyen's shadow arrived at the edge of the table. "Table fourteen," she said, and made a mark on her clipboard. "Tell me what I'm looking at."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
Anthony had told Felicity that Eid would fall in late June this year, the way it had the summer before, which was why he had shrugged off her question about the biology exam. Now he stood in the lobby of the cultural center with his tie already half undone, holding his phone open to the school calendar, and the two dates sat on the screen refusing to match. Eid was today. The exam on the immune system, antigens and antibodies and all of it, was tomorrow morning.

"You look like a man who has seen his own ghost," said Zaina, appearing beside him with a paper plate stacked so high with baklava that the plate had begun to bow in the middle. She followed his eyes to the phone. "Oh no. Not the bio exam."

"It was in summer last year," Anthony said. "I swear it was. We had the whole day, I didn't miss anything."

Zaina balanced her plate on the edge of the coat rack with the seriousness of a bomb technician. "Anthony. Think about your own life. When we were little, Ramadan was in the winter. I remember being jealous of you at school in December, getting to leave early. Now look outside." Outside, through the tall lobby windows, the April trees were in furious blossom, petals scattering across the parking lot like confetti somebody had thrown too soon.

Anthony turned his phone over and over in his hands, as if the answer might be on the back. "It moved. It just, moved." He said it slowly, testing the sentence the way you test a handrail. "It's not on the same date every year. It walks backward through the calendar."

"Eleven days or so, every year," Zaina said, plucking a piece of baklava off her stack and offering it to him like a consolation prize. "My dad counts down to it starting in like February. The Islamic calendar is lunar, and it runs about ten or eleven days short of the regular year, so everything comes earlier each time. You've been to, what, twelve Eids? You never noticed the dates marching backward?" She grinned. "You noticed the baklava quantities, though. I've seen you count."

He took the baklava because refusing felt like refusing a peace treaty. Through the open doors of the main hall he could see his mother at a table near the stage, laughing with three aunties whose combined volume could be heard from the street. His little cousin Omar was attempting to steal a samosa from a platter guarded by a grandmother, and losing, because Omar was small and determined and the grandmother was pugnacious in defense of her appetizers. Everything was warm and loud and exactly as it should be, except that at eight o'clock tomorrow morning he would be sitting in a hard plastic desk trying to remember the difference between an antigen and an antibody, and he had spent the evening he'd planned for studying on getting his shoes shined and his tie straightened.

"I could go home early," he said, and heard how weak it sounded even before Zaina raised one eyebrow.

"Your mother has been telling everyone her son is here. Mrs. Haq asked about you twice. You're leaving when the food leaves." She looked at him sideways. "Or you study here. There's a whole library downstairs. It's quiet, nobody goes down there during the party except the teenagers hiding from their relatives."

Felicity arrived at nine, pink-cheeked from the cold walk from the bus stop, holding a plastic bag. "I brought flashcards," she announced. "Also my mom's cardamom shortbread, which is not traditional, but which I maintain is thematically appropriate." She spotted the library door, wedged open with a folding chair, and led the way down like she owned the building.

They studied in the library under a lamp that hummed, and it was strange and good, the muffled party overhead, the occasional shriek of a child through the floor, Omar's distant pugnacious protests about bedtimes. Felicity quizzed him on immune response and he quizzed her, and when he got the antigen question wrong twice she made him stand up and act out a white blood cell, which he did with a commitment that drew actual applause from a passing teenager who had, in fact, been hiding from his relatives.

It was somewhere past ten, during a water break, that he pulled up a calendar site and started scrolling, year by year, forward. Zaina leaned over his shoulder. "What are you doing?"

"Checking next year. And the year after." He scrolled and scrolled, watching the festival dates creep backward across the months, out of spring, into winter, into the territory he half remembered from his childhood. "Ms. Friedman said something in September about planning ahead for exams. I thought she was being dramatic." He laughed at himself, quietly, because it was either laugh or wince. "She was being accurate."

"So next year you actually study before," Felicity said.

"Next year I check the dates before I open my mouth," Anthony said. "Two separate skills. I'm building both."

At eleven his mother found them, coats already gathered, Omar asleep against her shoulder like a sack of rice. She looked at the flashcards spread across the table, at the empty shortbread container, at her son, and something in her face went from suspicion to amusement without passing through anger at all. "You studied. At Eid." She said it like a diagnosis. "Your grandmother will say I'm too soft. She'll also say she's proud, but loudly, so everyone hears the soft part."

"Can I go in late tomorrow?" Anthony asked. "Just first period. I'll take the bus at seven."

She considered it, weighing him with her eyes, and then she acceded, but on her terms: "You'll eat breakfast first. Real breakfast, not a granola bar on the bus. And you'll text me after." She hoisted Omar higher. "Now come say goodbye to the aunties, or they'll ask about you all year."

He rode home in the back seat with his flashcards face-down on his knees, watching the streetlights slide across the glass, still not entirely sure he could tell an antigen from an antibody without closing his eyes first. Tomorrow would tell him. His mother turned up the radio to something old, and in the front seat Omar mumbled, half asleep, "Two samosas," and Anthony whispered back, "Three, if you're lucky."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
story:
The hardware store smelled of sawdust and machine oil, and by four o'clock the afternoon sun came through the front windows in long dusty bars. Noah had worked at Dang's Hardware since September, restocking washers and mixing paint, and he had learned that Mr. Dang trusted him with the register but not with the key to the cabinet of laminate samples, which was locked for reasons no one had ever explained.

The problem was the truck. Jacoby's cousin was selling a 2004 Ranger for two thousand dollars, and Noah had eight hundred in his desk drawer at home. He had been carrying the want around for weeks the way he carried the store keys, a small weight in his pocket he kept touching. On Saturday Jacoby came in to look at the paint chips for his mother's kitchen and leaned against the counter while Noah rang up a woman buying cabinet hinges.

"You should just put it on a credit card," Jacoby said after she left. "My brother did that. You pay it back slow, it's fine."

"Slow is the part that costs you," Noah said. "My dad still owes on a couch we got rid of two years ago."

"So save faster."

That was the incisive thing about Jacoby, that he could cut a problem down to one sentence and leave you standing there with it. Noah wiped the counter and thought about it for the rest of his shift, the smell of mineral spirits rising from the rag.

Sunday, Calum texted him a photo of a bank flyer, and they argued about it in messages.

Calum: ok this is stupid, the poster says 4.65 and then also 4.75, which is it

Noah: same account?

Calum: same account same poster. 4.65 compounded monthly, then 4.75 in big letters

Noah: so one of them is a lie?

Calum: the big number says APY under it. whatever that is

Noah lay on his bed with the phone on his chest and read the flyer again, zooming in. 4.65 percent, compounded monthly, 4.75 percent APY. He typed, deleted, typed again. He did not want to say something wrong to Calum, who repeated things.

On Monday he asked Mr. Dang, who was fishing a bent nail out of the key-duplicating machine. "Two different numbers for the same account," Noah said. "Four sixty-five and four seventy-five."

Mr. Dang squinted at the photo. "The big one is the APY," he said, and went back to the nail. That was all. Mr. Dang did not give speeches; he priced spackle and let you figure out the rest.

Noah figured out the rest at the picnic table behind the store during his break, eating a sandwich with paint under his fingernails. He read the flyer's small print twice, then a second bank's page on his phone, then a third. They all did it: a rate, and then a bigger number labeled APY. The APY, annual percentage yield, included the effect of compounding. That was why the same account could honestly say both numbers. He sat with that for a while, watching a sparrow work the cracks in the concrete for crumbs.

Then he understood the other half, and it arrived quietly, without triumph. Compounding was the same machinery that kept his father paying for a couch that no longer existed. Interest made borrowed money cost more over time, and it made savings grow, and the direction of the growth depended entirely on which side of it you stood. The bank was not lying to anyone. It was just describing a force, the way a weather report describes wind.

He texted Calum back: the 4.75 is the real yearly number once compounding counts. APY includes it. That's the whole trick. Then he counted it out on paper, eight hundred growing at that rate, how long to two thousand if he added most of every paycheck. Longer than he wanted. He thought about the credit card again, the couch again, the ease with which a person could subjugate his future self to his present self, signing a small agreeable form that made tomorrow's Noah into someone who owed.

He did not entirely trust his own reasoning. Maybe the truck would break down in a year and he would have saved for nothing. Maybe Jacoby's cousin would sell it to someone else this week and the whole question would dissolve. Causality ran forward, not sideways, and he could not see around its corner.

When his shift ended, Mr. Dang was locking the sample cabinet, and Noah stopped at the door with his jacket half on. "Can I pick up Sunday mornings too?" he asked. "Just through the spring."

Mr. Dang looked at him for a moment, then took the ring of keys off his belt and began opening the cabinet, as if the two things were connected. He pulled out a drawer of birch samples and set it on the counter.

"Your mother's kitchen," he said. "Which one is it? The pale one or the gray one."

Noah came back inside. "The pale one," he said, and put his jacket on the stool.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
story:
The line at the credit union had five people in it and one teller window open, so Mathis had time to reread the folded page in his hand, the printout his sister had shoved across the kitchen table that morning. Her student loan balance was larger than what she had borrowed, three years after graduation, even though she had never missed a payment. She had circled the number twice in red pen, hard enough to tear the paper.

He put the page away when Aya slid in beside him, backpack thumping the tile.

"You actually came," she said.

"I need the money before August. The program doesn't hold the spot."

The deposit for the summer robotics intensive was four hundred dollars, and the bus pass and the tool kit brought it to nearly six. He had two hundred and ten in his account and a mower and two lawns left before the season turned. The plan had been simple this morning. Borrow the difference, pay it back by September from his job at the garden center. Then his sister's page had arrived at breakfast, and simple had gone out of the room.

When his turn came, the teller brought up his account on the screen behind her. "You've got your youth savings," she said. "It's earned interest every quarter. Small amounts, but it compounds. It's added on, and then that earns interest too." She turned the monitor toward him so he could see the line of deposits, each one a few cents fatter than the one before.

"That's the savings part," he said. "I need the borrowing part."

She handed him a pamphlet and pointed him to the desk in the corner, where Mr. Ionescu, who had coached his sister's debate team and now, apparently, advised members on loans, sat with reading glasses low on his nose. Mathis laid out the number, the deadline, the September plan.

Mr. Ionescu didn't lecture. He slid a payment schedule across the desk and said only, "Read the third line."

Mathis read it. There was a column labeled interest, and a month where the interest wasn't paid, and a note in small type beside it: capitalized. "What's capitalized?" he asked.

"That's when unpaid interest is added to the loan's principal," Mr. Ionescu said. "From then on, interest is charged on the interest too."

Mathis sat back. His sister's page was in his pocket and he took it out and flattened it on the desk, next to the schedule, and the whole morning instantiated itself in front of him: her balance climbing not because she was careless but because of a mechanism built into the paper. She had deferred payments for a year after graduation, and the interest had not been forgiven or parked, it had been folded in, and it had started charging him its own rent.

"Wait," Aya said, leaning over his shoulder. She had followed him to the desk. "So her balance went up while she wasn't paying? That's the same word? Capitalized?"

"Same word," Mr. Ionescu said, and removed his glasses, and said nothing further, which was his way.

"So the same force that's growing my savings," Mathis said slowly, "grows her debt."

"It doesn't care which direction," Mr. Ionescu said. "You'd have to ask a philosopher whether it should."

Mathis looked at the schedule again. His loan was small and he would start paying in September, immediately, no deferral, nothing left unpaid long enough to fold in. But he thought about Aya, who wanted the littoral ecology field course in the fall, tuition due in December, and about his sister, and about the two hundred and ten dollars sitting in savings earning its patient cents. He could empty the savings and borrow less. Or he could leave it, let it work, and take the larger loan he was confident about today. Confident was a word he trusted less than he had at breakfast.

"I'll take three hundred," he said finally. "Keep the savings whole."

"Mathis." Aya pulled his sleeve. "You'll be short in July."

"I know."

"The deposit's nonrefundable."

"I know that too." He signed where Mr. Ionescu's finger rested, and the pen skipped once on the word borrowed. Outside, through the credit union glass, the July light lay flat on the parking lot, and he folded his sister's torn page into his pocket alongside his copy of the schedule, the two documents pressed together like evidence from opposite sides of one trial.

At the bus stop he called her. It rang four times.

"I found out what the word means," he said when she picked up. "On the statement. Capitalized."

A long pause, the sound of a cafeteria somewhere behind her.

"Read me the number again," he said. "The red one."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Connecting words such as Spanish 'sin embargo', meaning 'however', let a debater signal a counterargument clearly even when the rest of their grammar is simple.
story:
Grace had written her five minutes of Spanish on index cards, and now, reading them over in the corner of the language lab, she could hear the problem before she opened her mouth. The cards were a list. First, the dams cost too much. Second, the villages lose their land. Third, the fish disappear. Each sentence stood alone in her notebook like a stone on a windowsill, and the debate, which Ms. Buchanan would time with the clock on the wall, required her to sound as though the stones belonged to one wall.

"Ready?" Carmen asked, sliding into the chair beside her. Carmen had spent a summer in Quito and spoke with a looseness Grace envied, sentences that bent and recovered. Grace's sentences marched.

"Ask me the question again," Grace said. "The one about whether the country should build the dams."

Carmen asked it in Spanish, fast. Grace answered, and heard it happen again: a parade of points, no turns. Carmen frowned, not unkindly. "It's good," she said, "but you keep agreeing with yourself. Where's the other side?"

That was the real failure, Grace thought. She did have the other side in her head. Her father worked in power planning; she'd grown up hearing that without the dams the eastern towns burned diesel, that blackouts metastasize through a grid the way rumors move through a school, one failure dragging the next. She also had Carmen's aunt's letters, photographs of a drowned village, a church spire above the waterline. She held both positions, which was the honest way to be, and in English she could say so. In Spanish she could only stack them.

Ms. Buchanan moved between the rows, pausing at Giulia's desk, where a practice debate about city buses had dissolved into laughter over a mistranslated word. "Grace, you're up after Giulia. Use the full five minutes. If you stop early, stand there and think in Spanish."

Grace bent over her cards. Around her the room went on, Giulia arguing in her flat, determined accent, Carmen coaching someone two rows back, the clock's minute hand jerking forward. Grace wrote the word she wanted at the top of a blank card and stared at it: "sin embargo." She'd copied it off a handout weeks ago and never used it. She remembered Ms. Buchanan saying it once, quickly, tapping the page.

"What does it mean?" Carmen had asked then.

"However," Ms. Buchanan had said, and moved on.

Grace looked at it now and something shifted. However. It was a hinge. Her problem wasn't vocabulary or verbs; it was that she owned no hinges. A connecting word like "sin embargo" could signal a counterargument clearly even when the rest of the grammar stayed simple, and simple grammar was all she had. She didn't need perfect sentences. She needed turns.

She rebuilt the cards. The dams give light to the towns. Sin embargo, the villages lose everything. The fish will return, say the engineers. Sin embargo, no one knows the river after. Her Spanish was still plain, still slightly wrong in the gender of nouns, but the sentences now leaned against each other. She read it aloud under her breath and heard, for the first time, the shape of a person thinking rather than reciting.

"Giulia, excellent. Grace, stand up."

Grace stood. The clock began its sweep. She started badly, a mispronounced word, a stall over "grid," which she finally replaced by drawing a square in the air and saying "la red," hoping. Then the first card. The dams cost money, yes. Sin embargo, in her father's world, in the world of the eastern towns, the dark was worse than the debt. She made the turn and felt the room's attention turn with it. She gave the fish, the village, the spire above the water, then turned again: sin embargo, the town where a girl her age did homework by lamplight that failed twice a week.

By the fourth minute she was not reading the cards. She was arguing with herself in a borrowed language, plainly, with hinges, and the honest part was that she could not finish it. The last thing she said was that both things were true and she did not know how to choose between them, and she said it in Spanish that a child could have written.

The clock ran out. Ms. Buchanan wrote something in her book without looking up. Carmen turned around in her seat and mimed the hinge, two hands swinging open.

"After class," Carmen whispered, "you teach me that word."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
story:
The line at the Meridian Branch had six people in it and Brayden was fifth, holding his grandmother's deposit slip because she had twisted her wrist and refused, absolutely refused, to let a Saturday go by without the money going in. Above the tellers a muted television ran the noon news, and the closed captions marched along the bottom of the screen until a sentence caught him: FED RAISES RATES HALF A POINT. He read it twice. In economics class they had spent three days on inflation, and Ms. Mercado had made them write an essay on why raising interest rates was supposed to slow it, and he had written half of one and stalled.

He moved up one place. The man at the counter ahead of him was arguing about a hold on a check, and the teller, patient in that glazed professional way, kept saying the same sentence about funds availability. Brayden watched the captions change to weather. Half a point of what, though. That was the part he could not get past. He had written that people borrow less when rates go up, but he could not say whose rate, and when Ms. Mercado had circled his sentence and written "which rate?" in the margin, he had felt like a dilettante, someone skimming the surface of a thing he pretended to understand.

When his turn came he slid the slip and the envelope under the glass. The teller, whose name tag said NADIA, counted the bills with glacial patience, fanning them through the machine while he stood there. The television cycled back to the Fed story, a woman at a podium, and before he could talk himself out of it he asked, "Can I ask you something dumb. The Fed raised rates today. Which rate do they actually set? Like, is it mortgage rates? Credit cards?"

Nadia looked up. "Not dumb, actually." She glanced toward the desk where a personal banker sat with a client, then lowered her voice a little. "The Fed's main policy rate is the federal funds rate. That's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She said it briskly, the way she might have said the hold policy, and stamped the deposit receipt. "Everything else moves around it, mostly. But that's the one they set."

"Overnight," Brayden said. "Banks lend each other money just for one night?"

"All the time. Reserves, at the Fed. It's how they stay balanced at the end of the day." She slid the receipt across. "You want this in your account or your grandmother's?"

"Her account. She's in the car." He took the receipt and then didn't move. "But how does that slow inflation? If it's just banks passing money back and forth overnight."

Nadia smiled a little, checking the line behind him. "That I can't give you the whole lecture on. But think about it. If it costs banks more to borrow, what do they charge everybody else?"

He stepped aside to the counter against the wall, where the deposit slips were, and took out his phone but didn't open it. Instead he took out the folded essay from his back pocket, the one Ms. Mercado had marked up, and smoothed it on the cold marble. He read his own sentence: When interest rates rise, borrowing decreases and spending cools. Then he read her question again. Which rate. He found a pen chained to the counter.

At the little table by the door, an older man was filling out a slip with a magnifying glass, working at his own pace, and Brayden sat down across from him without asking. On the back of his essay he wrote: The Fed sets the federal funds rate. Banks charge each other this for overnight loans of reserves. Then, underneath: It's not mortgage rates. It's not credit cards. It's the base everything else stands on. He stopped. Was that true? Nadia had said everything else moves around it, mostly. Mostly. He underlined the word, then crossed the underline out.

He texted Maksim, who was in the class with him: do you know which rate the fed actually raised today. Maksim wrote back three minutes later: mortgage rates i think?? why. Brayden typed: no, federal funds rate, banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves. teller at the bank. Then he sat with the phone in his hand, rereading it, wondering whether he was passing on something he half understood, whether repeating Nadia's sentence made it his. He added: i still don't get how it slows inflation all the way down to prices. working on that part.

He looked at the essay. The first half had been glib, confident in the way of someone who had read one summary at midnight. Maybe he could burnish it, take the weak claim out and put this in, the actual mechanism, the overnight rate at the bottom of the chain. Or maybe the mechanism was still beyond him, and honest was better than polished. He folded the paper in quarters and put it in the pocket with the phone, and went out through the doors into the parking lot, where his grandmother's car sat idling at the curb with its window down.

"There you are," she said. "Did they take my money?"

"They took it." He got in and pulled the seatbelt across. "Grandma. When you and Grandpa bought the house, what were rates like?"

She put the car in reverse, checking over her shoulder. "Terrible. Eighteen percent, almost. Why?"

He buckled the belt and watched the bank shrink in the mirror. "I'm rewriting something. Tell me the rest on the way home."
