fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
The assignment went up on the board on Monday: pairs would teach a fifteen-minute session to the ninth graders on consent, contraception, and where to get tested, and everyone would draw their topic from Ms. Demetriou's coffee tin. Grayson reached in and unfolded his slip against the desk. Condoms, the pill, and clinics. Rylie, beside him, drew consent and made a small theatrical bow, as though she'd been handed the moral high ground on a velvet cushion.

"You realize you're the entertainment now," she said. "Ninth graders will eat you."

"I'm not doctrinaire about it," Grayson said. "That's my whole strategy. No lectures. I just tell them what a clinic actually looks like."

He had a reason for that confidence, though he hadn't shared it, and didn't intend to. Two months earlier, on a Tuesday he could still feel in his stomach, he had sat in the waiting room of the county health clinic for forty minutes with a number folded in his fist, watching the door at the far end like it might open onto a verdict. He had gone alone. He had told no one, including the person whose name was on the form under "partner," and that silence had become a thing he carried around, heavy and shapeless, like a coat he couldn't take off indoors.

For three days he and Rylie built the session in the library after school, spreading pamphlets across the table. Rylie kept sliding hers toward him. "Yours are the interesting ones," she said. "Mine are all, respect means yes. Which is true, but it's not a fact you can hold in your hand."

He held one in his hand now, a folded sheet from the clinic's rack, printed with a small table of methods. He'd skimmed it the first time, in the waiting room, too fast to absorb anything. This time he read the line about the combined pill twice, then a third time, and read it out loud. "With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed." He looked up. "Seven. I would have guessed, like, one. Maybe zero."

Rylie leaned over. "That's typical use. Real people, real life."

He remembered the nurse then, the one who had come out to the waiting room calling numbers, and how she had said the same word twice to a girl in the row ahead of him: reminder, reminder, set a reminder. At the time he'd thought she was just being fussy. Now the number on the pamphlet seemed to explain her, or half to. He didn't know why the number was what it was, and the pamphlet didn't say, and he found he was all right with carrying that particular uncertainty. It was the not knowing that made the reminder worth setting.

On Thursday, Kaylin came to watch their rehearsal and played the part of a hostile ninth grader with unsettling enthusiasm. "Why would I go to a clinic," she said, feet up on the chair in front of her, "when I could just ask Google?"

"Because at a clinic there's a person," Grayson said, "who asks if you want to be tested, and you say yes or no, and either way they don't flinch." He heard his own voice go flat on it and stopped.

Kaylin lowered her feet. Rylie looked at him for a moment longer than was casual.

The session itself was Friday, fourth period, in the middle school annex. Twenty-three ninth graders, all forearms and squeaking chairs. Grayson made them pass the pamphlets around like evidence. He explained consent first, borrowing Rylie's material with credit, and then held up the clinic's fact sheet and said the number, letting it sit in the room without softening it. A girl in the second row raised her hand and asked, "Is seven a lot?"

"It's seven more than zero," Grayson said. "It's not my job to decide if that's a lot for you."

Afterward, in the emptying hallway, Rylie caught up with him at the water fountain. "You've been to one," she said. Not a question. "The clinic. You talked about it like the chairs."

He drank, slowly, buying time, and the fountain's thin stream seemed very loud. Two months of the coat, and here was someone tugging at the sleeve.

"Kaylin too?" he asked.

"She guessed before I did. She just didn't say it out loud."

Grayson straightened and wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist. Down the corridor, Ms. Demetriou was stacking chairs, and outside the windows the parking lot was filling with the buses. He thought about how the whole morning had gone out from him like a tide, all that careful teaching, and left this one thing dry on the sand.

"Everything came back fine," he said finally. "But I never told her. The person on the form. That I went."

Rylie said nothing for a moment. Then, "Are you going to?"

The late bell rang through the annex, and the last bus pulled around the loop. Grayson picked up his bag.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging 'ibid.' in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title.
story:
The paper was due Friday, and by Tuesday night Alice had spread the wreckage across the kitchen table: six books, a printed article, her grandfather's copy of a style guide with a cracked spine, and a first draft that Mr. Rossi had handed back with more red than she'd ever seen on her own work. Beside her, the laptop glowed on the citation he'd circled twice, the little word she had trusted all along. "Ibid," she said out loud, just to hear it. The kitchen stayed quiet except for the refrigerator's hum.

Her grandfather had given her the guide in September, before she'd even known what a research paper was. She could still see him at this same table, tapping the page with one crooked finger. "You cite the source once," he'd said, "and after that, ibid. Same place, same source. Clean and economical, like a good ledger." He'd kept books for a hardware store for forty years, and he'd been delighted that something of his world could codify hers. She had written her first footnotes that night, proud of the little word, proud of the inheritance.

Mr. Rossi had not been proud. Next to every ibid. in the margin he'd written "outdated," and next to the first one, "check the current edition." Alice had stared at the word until it stopped looking like a word at all.

She texted Brendon, who was doing the same assignment on labor unions, and he called her within a minute, his voice tinny against her ear where the phone lay between the books. "Yeah, he dinged me too. I looked it up in the library copy." She pulled the library's copy toward her, the seventeenth edition, published in 2017, and found the section on shortened citations, and there it was: the seventeenth edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging ibid. in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title. She read the sentence twice. "So it's not wrong exactly," Brendon said. "It's just that the rules moved and your grandfather's book didn't." She said goodbye without really deciding to.

For a while she sat with both books open, the old guide and the new manual, like two relatives at opposite ends of a table who agreed on everything important and still couldn't be seated together. Her grandfather's way wasn't sloppy; it had governed dissertations for generations. But the new way had its own logic, each note carrying just enough of itself that a reader never had to flip backward. She tried writing one of her footnotes the new way, Smyth, "River Trade," 44, and then the next, Smyth, "River Trade," 51, and saw how the page looked: slightly more crowded, slightly more honest, each citation standing on its own two feet.

"It's like homeostasis," Angie said when she came by after practice, stealing a slice of the apple Alice hadn't touched. "Your paper finds a new equilibrium, but it costs you the old one." Angie was taking biology and found ways to make everything about the body. Alice laughed, but the comparison stuck with her through the next hour as she rebuilt the footnotes one by one, deleting each little ibid. and setting the author and short title in its place. With every deletion she felt the strange double movement of learning something: gaining a method and losing a small certainty she'd been fond of. She suspected there was no way around it, and she also suspected that her grandfather, if she was honest, would say the same thing about double-entry bookkeeping when the calculators came.

She was on her second page of corrected notes when her mother drifted through for tea and paused at the old guide, its cover soft as cloth. "Grandpa's?" she asked, and Alice nodded, and for a moment neither of them said the obvious, that he'd been dead since June and the book still smelled faintly of his basement. "He'd want you to get the grade," her mother said finally, which was the kind of thing people said, and might or might not be true. It occurred to Alice that she couldn't actually know what he'd want, that his preferences were now as fixed as his edition, and that she was choosing the living rule over the dead one for reasons that were partly about Mr. Rossi and partly about something she couldn't name yet.

By eleven she had a new bibliography, alphabetized, hanging indents uneven but honest, and a page of notes she hadn't dared look at twice. Somewhere in the middle of Chicago's machinery, she'd found a sentence she still didn't fully understand, something about how a citation style is a habit a whole profession agrees to share, and she'd underlined it without deciding whether she agreed. Doubt like that seemed endemic to the whole enterprise: the more carefully she cited, the more she saw how much she was taking on trust. She stacked the old guide on top of the new one, cracked spine over bright cover, and left them both by the kettle where she'd see them in the morning.

"Okay," she said to the empty kitchen, and closed the laptop.

story:
Xavier spread his first paycheque on the kitchen table and held it flat with two fingers, as if it might blow away before he understood it. The gross pay said one number and the net pay said a much smaller one, and between them sat a column of abbreviations: FIT, FICA, SDI, each with its own subtraction. He had worked forty hours over two weeks at the garden centre, hauling bags of mulch until his shoulders burned, and now the paper seemed to be telling him that a portion of those hours had belonged to the government all along.

His mother set a mug of tea beside him and looked over his shoulder without touching the cheque. "Read it line by line," she said. "That's what your father did. Every one of those letters is a deduction. Federal income tax, that's FIT. FICA is the payroll tax that funds Social Security and Medicare." She tapped the edge of the table, twice, and went back to the stove.

He wrote the abbreviations in his notebook anyway, because hearing something once had never been enough for him. Under them he copied the amounts, then subtracted the deductions from the gross himself and arrived, after two tries, at the net. The arithmetic worked. Somehow that was the part that unsettled him, that the whole arrangement was so orderly.

Tristan arrived at eleven with his own news, dropping into the chair across the table with his phone face-up. He turned it toward Xavier: a laptop, silver, discounted on a retailer's site. "My dad says we drive up to Portland this weekend and buy it there," Tristan said. "No sales tax. He does it for anything big."

"Oregon doesn't have any?"

"None. There are five states with no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon." Tristan said it the way he recited football stats, flat and certain. "We're right here, so Portland it is."

Xavier thought of the receipts in his backpack, the ones from the gas station where he'd bought sandwiches after his shifts. Each one had a line for the sandwich and a line beneath it for tax, a few coins that added to something by summer's end. He had never considered that a whole state might simply not have that line. It felt less like a loophole than like a fact about geography, a thing true on one side of a river and not the other.

Last spring, before any of this, he had sat at this same table watching his mother fill out her tax return, the long form spread across two placemats. She had seemed morose that whole evening, quiet in a way he'd mistaken for anger until she looked up and said the return was actually good news; she was getting money back because she'd overpaid through the year. The government, she explained, returning what wasn't theirs. He remembered feeling oddly exculpated on her behalf, though he couldn't have said of what, as if she'd been accused of something and the paperwork had cleared her.

"It's not free, though," Xavier said now, pulling the laptop toward him on Tristan's screen. "Look at the gas, the drive, the time. It's like the cheque. Gross and net. The sticker price is the gross." He heard his own voice and worried he was lecturing, which was not the position he wanted; he genuinely didn't know yet which side of it he came down on.

"Fine, but the sales tax on this thing is like ninety dollars here."

"That's real. So is a tank and a half of gas and your dad's Saturday." He slid the phone back. "I'm not saying don't. I'm saying count it the way you'd read a paycheque, all the lines."

Ms. Côté knocked then, returning the measuring cups she'd borrowed, and paused at the table on her way out. She caught sight of the stub, the notebook, the two receipts Xavier had fished from his backpack and laid beside Tristan's phone. "Homework or earnings?" she asked.

"Both," Xavier said. "I'm trying to figure out how much of my mulch-hauling I actually keep."

She laughed and said the figuring never quite stopped, and let herself out. Tristan was already scrolling again, squinting at the retailer's site, and after a moment he turned the screen around once more, tapping a line that said taxes calculated at checkout.

"Depends where it ships, apparently," Tristan said. "Portland store pickup, no tax. Or they deliver here and charge ours."

"So drive up and pick it up."

"My dad wants to leave at seven. Saturday morning."

Xavier copied the five states into his notebook, under the deductions, and circled Oregon. Then he closed the notebook and said, "I'll come with you. I want to see a receipt with nothing on that line."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
story:
The rain began an hour after they finished pitching the tents, and by the time the five of them crowded under the tarp that Ms. Tse had strung between two pines, the fire had drowned and Parker's science worksheet had gone the texture of wet cloth. He held it at arm's length, the ink bleeding into itself, the graph of carbon dioxide over the last century dissolving into a grey smear.

"Perfect," Taya said, and she didn't mean the weather. "You had the only copy."

Parker spread the page flat on the cooler, where it stopped dripping. The data table beneath the graph was still legible if he squinted: the numbers climbing decade by decade, the line they'd drawn rising like a staircase toward the top corner of the page. The assignment was due Monday, and it required him to explain, in his own words, how greenhouse gases trapped heat, and to interpret the graph he could no longer fully see. He had put it off until the trip because he'd assumed he'd have three quiet evenings, a lantern, the whole explanation copied from the textbook into neater sentences.

Aikam was chewing a granola bar and watching the rain hammer the lake into a million small craters. "I could dictate it to you," he offered. "I read the chapter twice. I'm kind of an autodidact that way."

"You read it twice because you failed the quiz," Taya said.

"I read it twice because the first time it made me mad."

Parker looked up from the ruined page. "Mad how?"

Aikam leaned forward, elbows on his knees. "Because it's all, greenhouse gases bad, greenhouse gases destroying the planet. But if they're so bad, why is the Earth warm at all?" He waved a hand at the tarp, the rain, the grey water beyond it. "The Moon gets the same sunlight we do, more or less, and it's frozen rock. No atmosphere worth anything. So which is it? Are these gases a poison or are they the blanket?"

Parker started to say the textbook answer, the one about bad gases, and then stopped, because he realized he didn't actually know. He had memorized a mood, not a mechanism. The rain drummed overhead, and Ms. Tse, sorting dry noodles at the far end of the tarp, said nothing, though he could tell she was listening by the way her hands had slowed.

"Okay," he said. "Let's think about it for real." He turned the worksheet over to its blank side and borrowed Taya's pencil. "The chapter had one number I remember, because it was so weird. Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus eighteen degrees Celsius." He wrote it, the minus sign deliberate. "Instead of roughly fourteen. That's the whole ballgame, right there. Thirty-two degrees of warmth, just from gases doing their thing." Taya frowned at the page, then at the rain, doing the arithmetic in her head. "So without them we're the Moon," she said slowly. "Frozen solid. Nothing lives."

"Exactly," Aikam said, pointing at her with the granola bar. "So they're a good thing."

"But the graph," Parker said, and he turned the soggy worksheet back over, shielding the smudged staircase with his body. "That's what the graph is for. The natural effect keeps us at fourteen. But look at the line. It doesn't stay flat. It climbs. And it's not the blanket that's the problem, it's that we keep piling on more blanket." He traced the ruined curve with his finger, and even half-dissolved it rose, unmistakable, the shape of a century of change. Taya leaned in beside him, her wet braid dripping onto the cooler, and together they read what remained of the numbers, decade by decade, her pencil rewriting the labels where the ink had fled.

"So it's both," she said. "The thing that makes life possible, and the thing we've overloaded."

"That's what I'll write," Parker said. "That it isn't good or bad. It's a system, and the graph is the system going out of balance." He paused. "I still don't fully get how the gases actually hold the heat. The chapter lost me there, something about molecules and energy, and I don't want to fake that part. I'll say what I know and mark what I don't."

Aikam grinned. "The autodidact is willing to admit ignorance. Mark the date."

The rain thinned to a whisper, and through the torn edge of the clouds the late sun found the lake, turning the whole surface to hammered brass. Steam lifted off the rocks where the day's warmth had been trapped, and Parker watched it rise, and thought, not unhappily, that the atmosphere was doing its quiet work right above him, melancholic weather and all, holding the world at fourteen degrees while they sat in it. Ms. Tse lit the stove, and the blue flame ionized the dusk air with the smell of boiling water and noodles.

"Get your paper," she said. "Write it while the light holds."

Parker pulled the worksheet onto his knee, pressed the pencil down, and wrote the first true sentence of the assignment: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus eighteen degrees Celsius. Behind him, Taya read it aloud over his shoulder, her voice low, like she was testing the weight of it.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness.
story:
The line at the bank moved slowly enough that Gavin had memorized the poster behind the tellers, the one with the lighthouse and the words about steady saving. He was there to withdraw the last hundred and forty dollars of what he had earned bagging groceries since October, because the driving test cost ninety, and the practice hours cost gas, and his mother had said, quietly, over dinner, that she could cover the test but not the mistakes. Ahead of him in line stood Ms. Esposito, who had taught him sophomore English and still greeted him by his last name. She turned, saw him, and said, "Gavin. You look like a man on a mission," and he said, "Driving test Friday," and she said, "Mine was in 1987 and I still remember the parallel parking. I clipped the cone. Went home and practised in front of my father's church for a week."

The teller, a young guy with a lanyard, counted out the bills, and Gavin folded them into his wallet and walked out into the parking lot where Shiloh's Corolla idled at the curb, exhaust curling in the March air. Shiloh had agreed to let him practise for the cost of a coffee, which Gavin took as friendship, though he suspected it was also that Shiloh wanted someone to drive him to work when his shifts ended after the buses stopped.

They started in the empty lot behind the closed hardware store, where Gavin lined up between two shopping carts he had placed as curbs. "You're too far out," Shiloh said from the passenger seat, feet braced against the floor. "The instructor wants you close enough that a cyclist could still get by, but you're being polite to an imaginary second cyclist." Gavin reversed, turned, straightened, and clipped the second cart with the rear bumper, sending it rolling into a puddle. He got out, set it up again, and did it seven more times until the eighth attempt left the car close to the curb, straight, and neither of them laughing.

The harder part came on the highway, and Gavin had been avoiding it the way he avoided certain thoughts, by scheduling around them. Mikaella met them at the park and ride with her notebook, because she was the one in their group who read entire manuals for pleasure. She had written a page of notes in her small, prolix handwriting, every rule expanded into sub-clauses and exceptions, and she read from it as Gavin pulled onto the ramp. "Okay, so this is the one thing everyone fails," she said. "Not merging. Following distance. Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness."

"How do I know it's two seconds?" Gavin asked, and she said, "Watch the car ahead pass a sign or a shadow or anything fixed. Then count. One one-thousand, two one-thousand. If you get to the sign before two, you're too close." He tried it against a mile marker and reached it at one second flat, and he eased off the gas until the next marker gave him two full counts, the gap stretching out in front of him like something he had been standing too close to for years.

The irony, which Mikaella pointed out without cruelty, was that Gavin had spent the whole winter telling anyone who would listen that traffic rules were arbitrary, that speed limits were revenue, that driving was basically a system of polite lies. He had gotten the argument from a podcast, and he had liked how it sounded, and defending it at lunch had made him feel like someone who thought for himself. "And now you're counting one-thousands like a monk," Mikaella said. "So which is it?"

He let the question sit while a truck passed on the left and he checked his mirror, then his blind spot, then merged into the lane behind a grey hatchback, leaving room, matching speed. The two ideas had not actually been opposites, he was beginning to see, but he didn't want to say that out loud yet, because he wasn't sure he could say it without it sounding like surrender. "Maybe the rules are arbitrary," he said finally, "and they're still the ones that keep you from eating a hatchback." Shiloh said, "That's the most prolix way anyone has ever admitted I was right," and Gavin said, "That's not what prolix means," and Shiloh said, "It's not not what it means."

On Thursday it rained, and Gavin drove the highway again with Mikaella riding along, the wipers beating their steady two-count, and he lengthened the gap to four seconds, then five, watching the hatchbacks and the taillights ahead of him blur and sharpen. There was something in it that unsettled him, the way repetition could desensitize you to danger, and also the opposite, the way counting seconds made the danger newly real, every rain-darkened car ahead suddenly a thing that could stop. Mikaella asked him what he was thinking and he said, "That this is the first time I've liked being careful," and she said, "Don't get attached. Careful is boring," and he said, "Boring is alive."

On Friday morning he stood in the testing centre parking lot while the examiner, a heavyset woman with a clipboard, walked around the car and then got in and said, "Whenever you're ready." Gavin signalled, checked the mirror, and pulled out past the bank, past the lighthouse poster he could no longer see, and set up for the cones. The rain had stopped but the road was still wet, and as he reversed between the markers he counted under his breath, one one-thousand, two one-thousand, giving himself the same distance he would give anyone else.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The envelope from Camp Willowmere arrived on a Tuesday, thin and official, and Anais read it standing at the kitchen counter while her mother chopped peppers behind her. Counselor-in-training, Mondays through Fridays, eight weeks, minimum wage. She had wanted this for a year, since Alyvia came home from the same camp with her hair smelling of lake water and a story about a five-year-old who called her Miss Alyvia for an entire week without laughing once. Anais wanted work that mattered to somebody, even somebody three feet tall, and she had said as much on the application. Now the letter said orientation was Friday at nine, and she folded it into her back pocket and went to find her passport.

She did not have a passport. That discovery took twenty minutes of pulling shoeboxes off the top shelf of her closet, and by the end of it the floor was covered with middle school orchestra programs and a friendship bracelet Abygail had made her in seventh grade, but no passport, because she had never left the country. Her birth certificate was in a fireproof box in her parents' room, which was locked, and her mother was working the closing shift all week. She found her social security card eventually, bent into a near-miss square at the bottom of a junk drawer, and she told herself that would be enough. Employers wanted your social security number. Everyone knew that.

Friday morning the gym smelled of floor wax and bug spray. Mr. Morningstar, the program director, stood at a folding table with a stack of manila folders, and a dozen teenagers sat on bleachers with their knees drawn up. He was younger than Anais expected, maybe thirty, and he had a way of pausing before he spoke that made even roll call sound rehearsed. When her name came he handed her a folder and said, "Fill out Section 1 of the I-9 before you start today. Everyone has to complete it no later than their first day of paid work. It's federal." He moved on to the next name.

Anais sat on the lowest bleacher with the folder open on her knees. Section 1 wanted her name, her address, a checkbox about citizenship, and then, at the bottom, a warning in bold letters about documents. She read it twice. The form did not simply want her social security number. It listed things she could show, and the list branched like a tree: certain documents alone, or certain combinations, and her lone bent social security card was, as far as she could tell, half of one combination and nothing on its own. Her stomach performed a small, precise drop. She thought about driving home, forty minutes round trip, about the locked fireproof box, about her mother asleep by then after a closing shift.

Alyvia slid down the bleachers and dropped beside her. "Stuck?"

"I don't have the right papers. I thought the social security card was the thing, and it's not the whole thing." Anais kept her voice low. "I have it, but I need something with it. I don't know what I have."

Alyvia pulled out her own folder, already finished, and showed the page where she'd written a driver's license number beside the card number. "My mom made me gather everything last night. She said don't denigrate the paperwork, paperwork is how you prove you exist to people who don't know you." Alyvia grinned. "She talks like that."

Anais had her learner's permit in her wallet, the flimsy paper one from the motor vehicle office, and she laid it next to the social security card on the bleacher and looked at them side by side. Both had her face or her name. Neither felt like proof of anything except that she had once stood in two different government lines. But the form, as far as she could work out from its branching lists, wanted exactly this pair, and so the pair was what she had.

She carried the folder to the folding table, where Mr. Morningstar was uncapping a pen for the boy ahead of her. The boy was arguing, obdurate, insisting he could just bring something next week, and Mr. Morningstar said, gently but without moving an inch, "Today is your first day of paid work, so Section 1 has to be done today. That's just how it is." The boy stormed back to the bleachers, muttering that the whole thing was designed by misanthropes who hated teenagers specifically, and Mr. Morningstar smiled a little at that, the way you smile at weather you can't change.

When it was her turn, Anais set the permit and the card on the table. "I think these work together," she said. "I'm not a hundred percent sure I read the list right, so check it before I sign anything." It cost her something to say the second sentence, to admit she might have gotten it wrong in front of a man who would be her boss for eight weeks. Mr. Morningstar looked at the documents, then at her, longer than the documents deserved. "Good instinct," he said. "Most people just sign and hope." He tapped the citizenship checkbox. "You're a citizen, so check that one. Then sign and date. And Anais, if the signature doesn't match your permit, that's fine, nobody's handwriting survives high school."

She checked the box, signed her name, and dated it. Then she walked out onto the dock, where Alyvia was already sitting with her sneakers off and her feet in the lake, and a line of six-year-olds in orange shirts came shouting down the path behind them, and Alyvia turned and called, "Miss Anais, they're yours today."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a foreign key in one table, such as an order's customer ID, points to a primary key in another.
story:
Grandfather's kitchen smelled of toast and pencil shavings, and the ledger books were stacked on the table like small weathered bricks. Carter set his laptop beside them and opened the tutorial Ms. Novák had assigned over the break: two tables, one of customers and one of orders, and a question at the bottom in bold. Find the customers who have never ordered anything.

The plan had been Joanna's, mostly. She had texted him three times from her own grandmother's house, where the wifi was, in her words, an oligarchy run by an aunt who doled out the password like grain in a famine. She wanted the tutorial done by Sunday so they could pair up on the next unit, and she had made him promise, which was how Carter found himself in a different kitchen, being watched by a grandfather who had his own reasons for hovering.

"There are names in those books that never bought a thing," the old man said, tapping the top ledger. "Forty years of customers, and some of them I carried along like extra weight. I always meant to sit down and work out who they were." He had tried once, he admitted, with a ruler and two open pages, and had abandoned it somewhere in the nineties. Now he wanted the list before the new year, so he could make calls, or at least so he would know.

Carter typed his first query, joined the two tables, ran it, and got a list that included nearly everyone, including customers he knew had ordered constantly. He stared at it. The join had happily matched each order to its customer, but it had also left the quiet ones stranded somewhere outside the results entirely, invisible rather than listed. He texted Emile, who replied with a single thumbs up, which Carter chose to interpret as moral support.

The grandfather made tea and, while the kettle worked, hunted for his reading glasses, which had gone missing in a way that seemed to destabilize the whole room; he checked the same drawer four times, then the windowsill, then declared with dignity that he had never owned glasses. Carter, without looking up, angled his laptop so its case caught the overhead light, and the reflection showed the glasses sitting in the old man's shirt pocket. The grandfather put them on and said nothing, which they both understood to be a settlement.

What Carter needed, he realized, was not a bigger query but a smaller idea. The customers table had a column called customer_id, and every row's value was different, one per person, no repeats. The orders table had the same column name, but there the values repeated, the same number appearing over and over for a loyal buyer and not at all for the ones who never called. He scrolled the tables side by side, following one ID with his finger like a man tracing a thread through a drawer of threads. Then he said it out loud, half to the room and half to Joanna in absentia. "The customer ID over here is a foreign key. It points at the primary key in the other table, and the primary key uniquely identifies each row." The grandfather, drying a cup, nodded as though this were a fact about tractors.

The fix was to join on that column and then ask which customers had no matching row at all, the ones the join left behind. Carter ran it and got eleven names. He read them aloud. The grandfather came around the table with his recovered glasses low on his nose and stood there for a while. One name he recognized and dismissed, a man who had only ever come in for the free coffee. Another made him quiet. "Her husband died in the spring," he said. "I thought she was avoiding me." He copied the eleven names onto the back of an envelope in his careful draftsman's hand, and Carter watched him decide, somewhere in the middle of the list, that he would start with her.

Joanna texted at dusk to say the aunt had relented and the wifi was now a commons, and asked whether he'd figured out the query or wasted the day. Carter looked at the envelope, already folded into the old man's coat pocket, and typed back a maybe, which felt like the honest answer. The tutorial question wanted a single right answer, and he had found one, but the list on the envelope had turned out to be eleven different questions, and he didn't know yet what you were supposed to do with a result like that. The grandfather, shrugging into his coat, said, "I'll be back by eight. Keep the light on."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
The community centre smelled of chlorine from the pool downstairs and burnt coffee from the vending machine, and Violet spread her notes across a folding table beside the ping pong half-court, where Anson was already waiting with his laptop open and his tie pulled loose like someone who had dressed for a trial and regretted it. The regional civics debate was in five days, and their motion was the kind nobody at school wanted to touch: that a presidential system makes it too hard to remove a head of government. Violet had drawn the affirmative, which meant she had to argue against the constitution she'd stood up for every morning of grade ten, hand over heart, and she kept circling the same question without landing on it.

"Give me your strongest thing," Anson said. He was technically her opponent, but they'd agreed to spar honestly, because a soft rehearsal helped neither of them.

"In Westminster, the parliament can just withdraw confidence," she said. "The head of government goes, just like that. Nobody needs two-thirds of anything."

Anson twirled a pen. "You say that like it's obviously good. You could depose a prime minister because of a bad week."

She hadn't thought of it that way, and the not-thinking bothered her more than the argument did.

Their coach at the centre, Ms. Nikolaidis, had given them a key to the second-floor reading room, a damp carpeted place with encyclopedias nobody opened anymore. On Thursday, Violet went up alone and pulled the blue volume with the worn spine, looking for the vote she'd half-remembered from class, the one everyone jokes about. She found it, and copied it, and then sat for a long time without writing anything else, because the numbers did something to her throat. Thirty-five senators voted to convict. Two-thirds were needed. The acquittal came by exactly one vote. A president had come within a single senator of removal, and the bar had held. She copied it twice, checking, then underlined it, then felt obscurely like she'd underlined a grave marker.

She built her case around it. On Saturday she argued it at the centre for Sofia, who had come ostensibly to practise her own speech but mostly to eat vending machine crisps on the reading room sofa. "A two-thirds threshold means a substantial consensus before you overturn an election," Violet said, trying out Anson's ground, seeing how it fit in her mouth. "It makes the system impervious to panic, to faction." Saying it aloud, she discovered she half believed it, and that disturbed her too, because she'd meant it as a steelman, not a conversion.

"You can't argue both sides," Sofia said, crumpling the crisp packet.

"I'm not arguing both sides. I'm trying to find where the actual line is." Violet explained her emerging position: that a parliamentary system trusts the legislature's judgment continuously, a presidential system trusts the electorate's choice almost absolutely, and that each trust had to fail catastrophically before anyone admitted it had limits. Sofia said that sounded like refusing to choose, and Violet said maybe refusing to choose was the honest version, and they left it there, the room going amber as the sun dropped behind the parking lot.

The night before the debate, Anson texted her a photo of his case outline with the caption "bring your best, no mercy," and she smiled at it and went back to flashcards. It was only in the morning, at the centre, folding her notes into her folder, that she found the folded page Sofia must have slipped into her bag on Saturday. In Sofia's rounded handwriting it said: You said 34 to convict when you practised. It was 35. I checked because I'm nosy. Also you called it a majority at first, and it's not a majority thing at all, it's two-thirds, which is the whole point. If you say it wrong tomorrow you lose to the facts. Violet read it three times, her ears hot, and understood that Sofia had been listening more carefully than she herself had been speaking.

The debate itself was held in the centre's main hall, chairs in rows, Ms. Nikolaidis presiding with a stopwatch. Anson spoke first and well, painting removal-by-confidence as a rolling tantrum, a parliament governed by mood. When her turn came, Violet stood, laid out her cards, and gave the numbers exactly: in 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote, thirty-five senators voting to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed. "A single vote," she said, and paused, slowing herself down on purpose. "If you think that threshold protected the country from a rash majority, then one vote was the margin of wisdom. If you think it shielded a man the legislature plainly wanted gone, then one vote was the margin of failure. I can tell you the number. I can't tell you which it was, and I distrust anyone who claims they can."

Anson's rebuttal was sharp; he called her position a technocracy of the undecided, rule by people who refuse to rule. In her last statement she conceded part of it, kept part of it, and said she'd take the Westminster speed for genuine misconduct and the presidential wall for everything short of it, then admitted out loud that "short of it" was exactly where honest people disagreed. The judges conferred behind the timer. Sofia, in the second row, held up the folded page and gave a small, imperative thumbs-up. Ms. Nikolaidis stood, envelope in hand, and said the winner's name, and it wasn't Violet's. She gathered her cards slowly, and across the hall Anson was already watching her, holding out his hand.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream's surface speed typically reaches about 2.5 metres per second at its fastest, making it one of the fastest ocean currents.
story:
Anna had forty minutes before the planetarium van left the quarry parking lot, and the current map was still a smear of blue arrows in her hands. Mr. Menon had handed out the laminated sheets on the bus, telling them only that whoever could explain the map to him by the end of the trip would earn the last spot on the oceanography field study in Lisbon. Anna wanted that spot the way you want something you have not admitted out loud yet, quietly and constantly, like a song stuck behind the teeth.

The quarry had flooded decades ago, and the town used it now as a swimming hole ringed by pale rock. The class sat on the ledges while Mr. Menon set up his portable screen, projecting the map onto the flat face of the north wall. Warm currents ran red-orange, cold ones blue, and a thick warm ribbon wound up the Atlantic like a vein. Anna knew it was called the Gulf Stream. That was the end of her knowledge, and the end was nowhere near the end of the problem.

"It's a race," Nathan said, dropping onto the rock beside her. "You, Samy, and whoever else bothers. Menon loves this stuff. He'll ask follow-ups." Nathan had no interest in Lisbon; he wanted to swim before the bus back, and he kept glancing at the green water below as if it might leave without him.

Samy was already at the screen with her phone out, photographing the projection, cross-referencing. Samy worked like that, hoarding certainty. Anna worked the opposite way, by feel, and the two of them had been circling each other since eighth grade, neither exactly a detractor of the other, neither exactly a friend. "The arrows," Samy said without looking up. "Surface speed's marked in the legend. Two point five metres per second at its fastest. One of the fastest ocean currents there is."

Anna turned that over. Two and a half metres per second meant nothing to her until she started walking it off along the ledge, heel to toe, counting under her breath. She walked the length of the projection, turned, walked it back. Nathan watched her with his chin on his fist. "You look insane," he said.

"I'm seeing how fast it is," Anna said. "It's like this. If the water were walking, it'd be walking like this." She did it again, brisker, and Nathan got up and matched her pace, then beat it, jogging backward along the rock, and she had to grab his sleeve to stop him from going over the edge into the quarry water. He laughed. She didn't, but she was close.

"That's a nice trick," Samy said from the screen, and there was a barb in it, though a small one. "But speed isn't the question. The question is why northern Europe is warm, and you can't pace that out." Samy's phone was open to a diagram of the North Atlantic, heat arrows radiating off a red ribbon toward Norway, Britain, France. Anna came and stood next to her, and the two of them looked at the same image from two different distances, Samy at the detail, Anna at the shape.

Mr. Menon called ten minutes from the water's edge, where he was wading with his shoes off. Anna took the map to him, but she didn't go straight at the question. "The Gulf Stream moves warm water north," she said. "It runs about two point five metres per second at its fastest, which is one of the fastest ocean currents, which I know because I walked it." Menon's eyebrows went up at that, and she kept going before she lost her nerve. "So it's carrying heat, and the heat comes off the water into the air, and the wind carries it over Europe. Ireland has palm trees. Sort of. I've seen pictures."

"Sort of," Menon agreed. He dried his feet on a sock he'd apparently designated for the purpose, which was its own kind of commitment. "Now the hard part. Is it the whole story?"

Samy appeared at Anna's shoulder with the phone held out, a graph on it, winds curving. "The winds do a lot of it too," Samy said. "Some papers say the current isn't even the main reason." Anna felt the ground tilt a little. She had a whole explanation five seconds ago, and now the explanation had a rival, and the rival was standing next to her being right.

"Then say both," Nathan called from the ledge, already in his swimsuit, which was somehow the most decisive thing anyone had done all afternoon. "You're allowed, aren't you? Say both and say you're not sure which matters more. Menon, she's allowed, right?"

Menon looked at Anna instead of answering him, which was how he answered most questions. Anna thought about acceding to Samy's version, clean and graph-backed, and about clinging to her own, walked-off and warm. Neither felt like hers alone anymore. "The current brings the heat," she said slowly, "and the winds spread it, and honest answer, I can't tell you yet which one does more. The water's doing this, though." She paced it again along the shore, heel to toe, brisk, and Menon watched her feet the whole way.

"There's one spot left in Lisbon," he said, "for a student who can say that and mean it."

Samy stood very still, phone dark in her hand. Then she said, "I'll drive the pace count tomorrow. Fresh legs." Nathan hit the water off the high ledge with a slap that echoed off the quarry walls, and Anna folded her map along the red ribbon until it was small enough to keep.
